::: {.callout-note}
## FAIR contribution

The guide primarily supports the following FAIR principles:

**Reusable**

- Well-structured software is easier for others to understand, maintain, and extend.
- Consistent coding practices reduce the effort required to reuse software in new research projects.

**Accessible**

- Clear project organisation lowers the barrier for new users and contributors.

:::

# Why does software quality matter?

Research software often begins as a solution to a specific scientific problem, then grows in complexity as features, collaborators, and reuse accumulate. Poor quality rarely breaks it today—it just makes future changes slower, onboarding harder, and bugs harder to find.

Software quality can be summarised by one question:

> **Can someone else understand, modify, and trust this software?**

This guide focuses on practical improvements—project structure, readable code, review, incremental change, and long-term maintenance—that move you toward that goal without requiring a complete redesign.

---

# Principle 1: Organise your project consistently

As projects grow, files tend to accumulate wherever convenient, making it harder to see where functionality lives. A consistent structure answers basic questions for a new contributor: where is the source code, the tests, the documentation, the examples?

```text
my-project/
├── src/
├── tests/
├── docs/
├── examples/
├── LICENSE
├── README.md
└── pyproject.toml
```

Keep source, tests, documentation, and generated files separated, and keep configuration in predictable locations. See RSQKit's lesson on [software project structure](https://everse.software/RSQKit/software_project_structure) for more examples of project layouts.

---

# Principle 2: Write code for people

Code is read far more often than it is written. A few habits go a long way:

**Use descriptive names.**

```python
samples = load_samples("samples.csv")   # not: x = load("samples.csv")
```

**Prefer early returns over nested conditionals** ([guard clauses](https://refactoring.guru/replace-nested-conditional-with-guard-clauses)).

```text
if not A: return
if not B: return
if not C: return
...
```

**Keep functions focused**—one clear responsibility each, rather than one function that reads, filters, analyses, and exports.

**Remove unused code** rather than commenting it out—version control already preserves the history.

See RSQKit's lesson on [writing readable code](https://everse.software/RSQKit/writing_readable_code) for language-specific style guides and tooling (formatters, linters, type checkers) that help enforce these habits automatically.

---

# Principle 3: Have your code reviewed

A second pair of eyes catches what you are too close to see: unclear logic, an edge case you didn't consider, duplicated code that should be a shared function, or twenty lines that a well-tested library could replace in one.

## Automated code review

Automated tools complement human reviewers by catching mechanical issues before code is merged:

| Tool | Purpose |
|------|---------|
| [GitHub Pull Requests](https://docs.github.com/en/pull-requests) | Collaborative code review |
| [GitHub Copilot code review](https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/using-github-copilot/code-review/using-copilot-code-review) | AI-assisted review suggestions |
| [CodeQL](https://codeql.github.com/) | Detect security vulnerabilities and common coding mistakes |
| [Super-Linter](https://github.com/super-linter/super-linter) | Run multiple linters in one workflow |
| [Ruff](https://docs.astral.sh/ruff/) (Python) | Fast linting and formatting |
| [Pylint](https://pylint.readthedocs.io/) (Python) | Detect programming errors and style issues |
| [lintr](https://lintr.r-lib.org/) (R) | Check R code for style and common issues |
| [clang-tidy](https://clang.llvm.org/extra/clang-tidy/) (C/C++) | Static analysis for C and C++ |

Automated tools are fast but cannot judge whether an implementation fits the scientific problem—combine them with human review. See RSQKit's lesson on [code review](https://everse.software/RSQKit/code_review) for how to run an effective review process.

---

# Principle 4: Improve your software incrementally

Research software evolves alongside the research questions behind it. Large rewrites are rarely practical, but small improvements fit naturally into everyday work:

- fixing a bug is a chance to also clarify the function around it;
- adding a feature is a chance to move related logic into its own module before it gets crowded;
- reviewing code is a chance to flag a missing docstring or unclear name, not just the issue at hand.

These small improvements accumulate, and are far easier to sustain than occasional large refactoring efforts. See RSQKit's lesson on [maintaining research software](https://everse.software/RSQKit/software_maintenance) for concrete ways to track technical debt, such as issue-tracker labels and protected refactoring time.

---

# Principle 5: Plan for long-term maintenance

Research software often outlives the project that funded it. Dependencies age, platforms change, and the person who understood the code best may move on before the software stops being used.

Maintenance work generally falls into a few recurring categories:

| Type | Trigger | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Corrective | A bug is discovered after release | Fixing an edge case reported by a user |
| Adaptive | The environment around the software changes | Updating code for a new Python or OS version |
| Perfective | Feedback suggests an improvement | Speeding up a slow analysis step |
| Preventive | A recurring risk is identified | Refactoring a fragile module before it causes issues |

Two habits make this manageable rather than overwhelming:

- **Pin and periodically update dependencies.** Unpinned dependencies can silently break your software when a new release changes behaviour; pinning avoids surprises, but only if you also revisit those pins occasionally rather than never. See RSQKit's lesson on [maintaining research software](https://everse.software/RSQKit/software_maintenance) for language-appropriate pinning tools.
- **Be explicit about maintenance status.** If a project is no longer actively maintained, say so in the README—far more useful to future users than letting them discover it through unanswered issues. [repostatus.org](https://www.repostatus.org/) provides a standard set of badges for declaring this.

See this [overview of software maintenance types](https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/software-engineering/software-engineering-software-maintenance/) for more detail on the categories above.

# Common pitfalls

## Optimising too early

[Premature optimisation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Program_optimization) often makes code more difficult to understand. Write code that is correct and maintainable first, and optimise only when measurements show it is necessary.

## Chasing perfect architecture

Research software evolves alongside research questions. Design your software so that it can change, rather than trying to anticipate every future requirement—the [YAGNI principle](https://martinfowler.com/bliki/Yagni.html) ("You Aren't Gonna Need It").

## Ignoring technical debt

Shortcuts are sometimes necessary, but leaving them in place indefinitely, unrecognised, makes future development more difficult. See Martin Fowler's [explanation of technical debt](https://martinfowler.com/bliki/TechnicalDebt.html) for how to reason about when a shortcut is acceptable. For a nice read on where the metaphor came from and how it's often misused in practice, see ["Technical Debt: The Man, the Metaphor, the Message"](https://neopragma.com/2019/03/technical-debt-the-man-the-metaphor-the-message/).

---

# Take-away

Maintainable software is not the result of one large refactoring effort. It is the result of many small decisions that make code easier to understand, modify, and review—and of planning for the maintenance that continues long after the initial development is done.

---

# Checklist

Consider the following questions:

- Does your project have a consistent directory structure?
- Can a new contributor quickly identify where important files are located?
- Are variables and functions clearly named?
- Do functions have a single responsibility?
- Is code written for readability rather than cleverness?
- Are important changes reviewed before they are merged?
- Do you use automated code quality tools where appropriate?
- Do you make small improvements as part of your normal development workflow?
- Are your dependencies pinned, and revisited periodically rather than never?
- If the project is no longer actively maintained, does the README say so?
